# Music for sociocultural and political expression
## The area of inquiry
This area of inquiry studies music that expresses the identity, beliefs and politics of a group. Examples include protest songs, national anthems, music for religious worship and music of social movements.

## Examples
Protest songs such as those of the US civil rights movement used simple melodies and call-and-response so many people could join in. Anthems use strong rhythms and memorable tunes to build unity. Context is the cultural, historical and social situation in which music is made and heard.

## Elements of music
The elements of music are pitch, rhythm, tempo, dynamics, timbre, texture, harmony and structure. Melody is a sequence of pitches heard as a line. Texture describes how layers combine: monophonic, homophonic and polyphonic.

## Key terms
Area of inquiry: a broad category used to study music
Protest song: a song that expresses opposition to injustice
Call and response: a phrase answered by another phrase
Context: the situation in which music is made and heard
Texture: how musical layers combine
Music for listening and performance:
# Music for listening and performance
## The area of inquiry
This area of inquiry studies music written mainly to be listened to and performed, such as concert music, chamber music and solo repertoire. It looks at how composers and performers shape structure and expression.

## Concepts
Form is the overall structure of a piece, such as binary (AB), ternary (ABA), rondo (ABACA), theme and variations, and sonata form. Interpretation is how a performer realizes the score through tempo, dynamics and articulation. An ensemble is a group of performers.

## Elements of music
The elements of music are pitch, rhythm, tempo, dynamics, timbre, texture, harmony and structure. Melody is a sequence of pitches heard as a line. Texture describes how layers combine: monophonic, homophonic and polyphonic.

## Key terms
Form: the overall structure of a piece
Ternary form: an ABA structure
Sonata form: exposition, development and recapitulation
Interpretation: how a performer realizes the score
Ensemble: a group of performers
Music for dramatic impact, movement and:
# Music for dramatic impact, movement and entertainment
## The area of inquiry
This area of inquiry studies music that supports drama, dance, film, games and entertainment. Music can create mood, depict characters and drive action.

## Concepts
A leitmotif is a short musical idea linked to a character, place or idea, used by Wagner and in film scores. Diegetic music is heard by the characters; non-diegetic music is heard only by the audience. Dance music uses a strong beat and regular phrases for movement. Underscore is background music that supports a scene.

## Elements of music
The elements of music are pitch, rhythm, tempo, dynamics, timbre, texture, harmony and structure. Melody is a sequence of pitches heard as a line. Texture describes how layers combine: monophonic, homophonic and polyphonic.

## Key terms
Leitmotif: a musical idea linked to a character or idea
Diegetic music: music the characters can hear
Non-diegetic music: music only the audience hears
Underscore: background music supporting a scene

# Music technology in the electronic and digital age
## The area of inquiry
This area of inquiry studies how technology changes how music is created, performed and shared. Examples include electronic dance music, hip hop production, film scores and music for games.

## Concepts
A digital audio workstation (DAW) is software for recording, editing and producing music. Sampling is reusing part of a recording in a new piece. Synthesis creates sounds electronically. MIDI is a protocol for sending musical data between devices. Effects such as reverb, delay and distortion change timbre.

## Elements of music
The elements of music are pitch, rhythm, tempo, dynamics, timbre, texture, harmony and structure. Melody is a sequence of pitches heard as a line. Texture describes how layers combine: monophonic, homophonic and polyphonic.

## Key terms
Digital audio workstation: software for recording and producing music
Sampling: reusing part of a recording in a new piece
Synthesizer: an instrument that creates sounds electronically
MIDI: a protocol for sending musical data
Reverb: an effect that adds a sense of space
Exploring music in context:
# Exploring music in context
## Exploring
Exploring music in context is the process of investigating diverse musical material through listening, analysis and research. You study music from different cultures and times through the four areas of inquiry.

## Doing it well
Analyse how musical elements work in each piece and how context shapes them. Compare pieces from different contexts. Use subject-specific vocabulary and cite your sources. This feeds into the exploring music in context assessment, which presents your findings with written work and practical exercises.

## Key terms
Musical analysis: examining how the elements of music work in a piece
Diverse musical material: music from a range of cultures and times
Subject-specific vocabulary: technical musical terms
Cultural context: the culture in which music is made
Experimenting with music:
# Experimenting with music
## Experimenting
Experimenting with music is the process of applying what you learn to your own creating and performing. You experiment with techniques, styles and ideas from the music you study.

## Doing it well
Document your experiments, explain the musical choices and reflect on the outcomes. The experimentation report presents creative and performance experiments with evidence such as recordings and scores. Reflection is evaluating what worked and what you would change.

## Key terms
Experimentation: trying out musical techniques and ideas
Experimentation report: the assessment documenting your experiments
Reflection: evaluating what worked and why
Score: written notation of music
Presenting music:
# Presenting music
## Presenting
Presenting music is sharing your finished work as a composer and performer. The musical presentation includes finished compositions and performances, with programme notes.

## Doing it well
Choose pieces that show your range and skill. Rehearse thoroughly and pay attention to accuracy, expression and communication with the audience. Programme notes are short written texts that give the audience context and explain your intentions.

## Key terms
Musical presentation: the assessment of finished compositions and performances
Programme notes: short texts giving context for a performance
Composition: an original piece of music
Rehearsal: practice before a performance
Stage presence: communicating confidently with an audience
The contemporary music-maker:
# The contemporary music-maker
## The HL project
The contemporary music-maker is an HL component. You plan and carry out a collaborative real-life music project, taking on roles such as composer, performer, producer or researcher.

## Doing it well
Define a clear project and your role. Plan the stages, collaborate with others, and document the process in a continuous multimedia presentation. Evaluate the project against your goals and reflect on what you learned about being a music-maker today. Collaboration means working with others towards a shared goal.

## Key terms
Contemporary music-maker: the HL collaborative project component
Collaboration: working with others towards a shared goal
Producer: a person who oversees the making of a recording
Project proposal: a plan setting out the project’s aims
